title: Care and Monitoring of Critically Ill Patients

headings.title: Introduction to Critical Care Nursing and the ICU Environment
headings.content: Critical care nursing focuses on patients experiencing life-threatening health problems requiring complex assessment, high-intensity therapy, and continuous intervention. The Intensive Care Unit houses specialized monitoring technology, mechanical ventilators, and infusion pumps designed to sustain failing organ systems. Maintaining patient safety in this high-stress environment demands relentless vigilance, rapid clinical decision-making, and seamless interprofessional collaboration among physicians, physiotherapists, and nurses. Patient-to-nurse ratios are deliberately kept low, often one-to-one or one-to-two, reflecting the sheer volume of tasks and the constant need for dynamic physiological adjustments.

headings.title: Physiological Assessment and Systematic Evaluation
headings.content: Systematic evaluation of unstable individuals relies on structured frameworks. The **ABCDE approach**—Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, and Exposure—ensures life-threatening issues are identified and managed before moving to secondary assessments. Baseline neurological status, peripheral perfusion, and hourly urine output serve as vital indicators of systemic tissue oxygenation and organ function. Subtle trend changes often signal impending shock or sepsis long before catastrophic collapse occurs.

headings.title: Hemodynamic Monitoring and Cardiovascular Support
headings.content:
Hemodynamic monitoring provides direct insight into heart function and vascular tone. Invasive lines, such as arterial catheters and central venous pressure lines, generate real-time data regarding blood pressure and intravascular volume status. 

- **Arterial Line**: Offers continuous blood pressure monitoring and easy access for frequent arterial blood gas sampling.
- **Central Venous Pressure (CVP)**: Measures filling pressures in the right atrium, guiding fluid resuscitation strategies.
- **Vasopressors**: Medications like norepinephrine constrict blood vessels to restore adequate perfusion pressure in distributive shock.

headings.title: Respiratory Management and Mechanical Ventilation
headings.content:
When respiratory failure occurs, mechanical ventilation takes over the work of breathing. Nurses must manage ventilator circuits, monitor peak inspiratory pressures, and assess arterial blood gases to evaluate oxygenation and ventilation adequacy. 

Maintaining a patent airway requires meticulous endotracheal suctioning using sterile technique, keeping the head of the bed elevated between 30 and 45 degrees to prevent aspiration, and providing comprehensive oral care with chlorhexidine to ward off ventilator-associated pneumonia.

headings.title: Neurological Monitoring and Management of Intracranial Pressure
headings.content: Neurological deterioration can happen rapidly in brain injury, stroke, or post-cardiac arrest states. The **Glasgow Coma Scale** evaluates eye opening, verbal response, and motor activity to track changes in consciousness over time. When intracranial pressure rises due to edema or hemorrhage, cerebral perfusion pressure drops, threatening ischemic brain damage. Nursing interventions include maintaining neutral neck alignment, avoiding sudden hip flexion, administering prescribed osmotic diuretics like mannitol, and minimizing environmental stimuli.

headings.title: Fluid Balance, Electrolyte Management, and Nutritional Support
headings.content: Balancing inputs and outputs forms a cornerstone of critical care nursing. Fluid overload can precipitate pulmonary edema, while hypovolemia triggers renal failure. Electrolyte derangements—particularly potassium, sodium, and calcium—pose lethal risks for cardiac arrhythmias. Simultaneously, early enteral nutrition via nasogastric or post-pyloric tubes preserves gut integrity and blunts hypermetabolic stress responses, though parenteral nutrition serves as a backup when the gastrointestinal tract is entirely non-functional.

headings.title: Medication Safety, Sedation, and Pain Management
headings.content: Managing pain and anxiety while avoiding over-sedation is a delicate balancing act. Validated tools like the **Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale** help target appropriate comfort levels so patients can participate in spontaneous breathing trials. High-alert medications—such as insulin, opioids, and inotropes—demand rigorous double-check procedures before administration. Nurses must remain vigilant for withdrawal symptoms, delirium, and respiratory depression during continuous infusions of sedative agents.

headings.title: Prevention of Complications: Infection Control, Pressure Injuries, and VTE
headings.content: Critically ill patients face compounding threats from immobility and invasive devices. Catheter-associated urinary tract infections and central line-associated bloodstream infections are minimized through strict aseptic technique and daily necessity reviews. Regular repositioning every two hours, combined with specialized support surfaces, protects fragile skin integrity. Additionally, pharmacological prophylaxis with low-molecular-weight heparins or mechanical compression devices guards against deep vein thrombosis.

headings.title: Ethical Considerations, End-of-Life Care, and Family Support
headings.content: Critical care nursing intersects frequently with profound ethical dilemmas, including decisions surrounding life-support withdrawal, do-not-resuscitate orders, and surrogate decision-making. Nurses advocate for patient autonomy and comfort when curative treatments are no longer viable. Providing compassionate end-of-life care involves managing symptoms like dyspnea and pain aggressively while offering emotional presence and clear communication to distressed family members navigating sudden loss.
